quizzes.title: Module Intro: Before You Begin
quizzes.description: Welcome to this module. This short survey is not graded for correctness. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting.

questions.text: When a country has no rival, what keeps it from becoming careless? Give your best answer now. You will come back to this question at the end of the module.

This module has these goals. Read them, then choose one answer.

  • Describe the Persian Gulf War and why the United States built a coalition to fight it.
  • Explain the ideas behind the free trade agreements and the economic boom of the 1990s.
  • Evaluate the limits of American power after the Cold War.
  • Describe the growing threat of terrorism against Americans in the 1990s.
  • Explain the debate over immigration and the laws passed to address it.
  • Explain how the election of 2000 was decided and what it shows about American institutions.

answers.text: I have read the goals and I understand what this module asks of me.
I have read the goals, but I have a question about one of them.

questions.text: Some assignments in this course allow you to work with classmates. How do you plan to work this module?

answers.text: I would like to work with a group when that is an option.
I would rather work on my own.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: The Post-Cold War World
quizzes.description: Answer each question using what you learned in this week's two lessons. You may look back at them, but the answers are not stated word for word. You will need to put facts together.

questions.text: Before the Gulf War began, President Bush went to the United Nations and to Congress. Which choice best explains why this set the war apart from the way the country entered the Vietnam War?

answers.text: Congress declared war before Iraq invaded Kuwait.
A group of allied nations joined the effort, and Congress voted to approve the use of force before the fighting began.
The United Nations commanded the American army.
Bush won the approval of the nation by keeping the plans secret.

questions.text: When the coalition drove the Iraqi army out of Kuwait, Bush stopped and did not march on Baghdad. Which reason does the lesson give for that decision?

answers.text: Congress had ordered him to stop by a vote of 52 to 47.
The Iraqi army was too strong to defeat.
American soldiers refused to go farther.
He feared that removing Saddam would break the coalition and leave America in charge of a hostile country.

questions.text: Which person would most likely have opposed NAFTA?

answers.text: A consumer who hoped to buy cheaper goods.
A company that wanted to sell its products in Mexico.
A worker in a town whose main factory might move to Mexico.
A trader who wanted to open new markets abroad.

questions.text: After the battle in Mogadishu, Clinton pulled American troops out of Somalia. Later, in Rwanda, the world did not act to stop a genocide. What did American leaders take away from these events?

answers.text: They should send large armies wherever people were suffering.
They should be slow to send troops to places where no vital American interest seemed to be at stake.
The United Nations should take over American foreign policy.
The military was too small to fight any war at all.

questions.text: In the 1990s, officials warned of a larger terrorist threat, yet the government did not stop the attacks that came. Which pair of facts from the lesson helps explain why?

answers.text: There was no agreement on what to do, and agencies such as the CIA and FBI had trouble sharing information.
The attackers were all American citizens, and Congress had banned all investigations.
Bin Laden was in prison, and the embassies were closed.
The Cold War had ended, and no weapons were left to use.

questions.text: The Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 offered amnesty and banned the knowing hiring of people without legal status. Why did illegal immigration keep growing afterward?

answers.text: The amnesty was withdrawn after a year.
Courts struck down the law the day it passed.
Congress repealed the law in 1990.
Employers found ways around the rules, and enforcement was weak.

questions.text: Gore disagreed with the Supreme Court's decision in Bush v. Gore but said he would respect it. Why does the lesson say that this tells us something about the health of the republic?

answers.text: It proved that the Court's decision was fair to everyone.
It showed that Gore had never really wanted to be president.
A disputed election, settled by lawyers and judges, ended with a peaceful transfer of power and no one calling out the army.
It meant that the Electoral College was no longer needed.

questions.text: The 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center killed six people, and the towers did not fall. Why did it change so little about how most Americans thought about their safety?

answers.text: Few people lived in New York.
The men were caught and tried in court, and many Americans saw the case as a crime to be punished rather than as a war.
The government kept the attack a secret.
Bin Laden had already been arrested.

quizzes.title: Module Outro: Looking Back
quizzes.description: You have finished this module. Please answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see how the class is doing.

questions.text: Look back at the question from the start of the module. When a country has no rival, what keeps it from becoming careless? Give your answer now, using at least one fact from this module. You may say if your thinking has changed.
How confident do you feel about the material in this module?

answers.text: Very confident. I could explain it to someone else.
Fairly confident. I understand most of it.
Somewhat unsure. I understand parts of it.
Not confident. I need help.

questions.text: What is still unclear to you? Name a person, event, or idea. If nothing is unclear, write "nothing."
Which of these did the people in this module most need, whether they had it or not?

answers.text: Courage
Courtesy
Honesty
Perseverance
Self-government
Service
Responsibility

questions.text: Pick one person from this module (George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton, Al Gore, the sailors of the USS Cole, or someone else) and explain, in two or three sentences, how that virtue showed up in what they did, or how its absence did.

discussions.title: Discussion: The Post-Cold War Peace: Real or a Pause?
discussions.html:
For many Americans, the 1990s felt like a holiday from history: no rival, a booming economy, and a quick victory in the Gulf. Yet dangers were growing in plain sight. Was the peace of the 1990s real, or only a pause?

Your post (about 100 to 150 words):

  1. Take a clear position: the peace was real, it was a pause, or a mix that leans one way.
  2. Give one specific piece of evidence from the lesson "The Unipolar Moment: War, Trade, and Boom" or the source George H. W. Bush, Address to Congress on the Persian Gulf Crisis that supports you.
  3. Name one fact that cuts against your position, and explain why you still hold it.

Your reply (about 50 to 75 words): Respond to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with something they did not use. If not, say respectfully where their reasoning falls short.

Post first, then reply. You will not see your classmates' posts until you have posted.
